sentences.text: "Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
If so, to what amount and from whom?

16. As the issue no.1 has been proved in affirmative and in favour of the petitioner, the petitioner has become entitled to be compensated for the injuries suffered in the above accident, but the computation of compensation and liability to pay the same are required to be decided.
17. In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. Pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.

The "pecuniary damages" or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by her in the accident.
The "non-pecuniary" or general damages are those damages which are incapable of being PANKAJ by PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.06.04 13:27:00 +0530 assessed by arithmetical calculations.

The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc. and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.

It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate her or to put her almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating her is also not to reward her or to make her rich in an unjust manner.

It is also well settled that the 'just' compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.

Further, in case of permanent disability, the assessment of compensation under the head of loss of future earning, would depend upon the effect and impact of such permanent disability on his earning capacity.

Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India)

sentences.text: (iv) Loss of future earnings due to disability 22.
Petitioner claimed in her affidavit Ex. PW1/A that she has become permanently disabled after the accident and could not perform her work any more.
As per disability certificate Ex. PW-1/4, the petitioner has suffered 16% permanent physical impairment with respect to left lower limb which is non progressive and not likely to improve in future.
From the facts it is evident that the petitioner has suffered permanent physical impairment in relation to her left lower limb to the extent of 18%.
As a matter of fact the petitioner was working as a beautician and due to physical disability her working capacity has reduced to a greater extent.
She has stated in her evidence that she is unable to work and as of now she is workless.
On behalf of petitioner it was urged that her functional disability be considered 100% as her permanent disability in the left lower limb has made her incapacitated to perform her work.

As per evidence the petitioner is 10 th pass and she got training of PANKAJ PANKAJ SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.06.04 13:27:17 +0530 beautician in local beauty parlour and thereafter was working as a beautician for her living.
The petitioner has no other professional degree to use her for her living.
The evidence of PW-2 Dr. Sanjay Yadav also suggests that petitioner's disability is permanent in nature and there is no chances of reduction in the disability.

Therefore, considering totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of considered view that considering the age, vocation and qualification in the back drop of her permanent disability it would be apposite to consider her functional disability as 50%.
This Tribunal has already assumed the monthly income of petitioner to be Rs. 20,357/- at the relevant time.

In view of the above discussion, this Tribunal is constrained to hold R-1 guilty of gross negligence and default in driving the offending vehicle at the relevant time.
17. In terms of provisions contained in Section 168 of the MV Act the compensation which is to be awarded by this tribunal is required to be 'just'.
In the injury cases a claimant is entitled to two different kinds of compensations i.e. Pecuniary as well as non-pecuniary damages.
The "pecuniary damages" or special damages are those damages which are awarded and designed to make good the losses which are capable of being calculated in terms of money and the object of awarding these damages is to indemnify the claimant for the expenses which he had already incurred or is likely to incur in respect of the injuries suffered by her in the accident.
The pecuniary or special damages generally include the expenses incurred by the claimant towards his treatment, special diet, conveyance, cost of nursing/ attendant, loss of income/earning capacity etc. and the non- pecuniary damages generally include the compensation for the mental or physical shock, pain and sufferings, loss of amenities of life, marriage prospects and disfiguration etc.
The above categories falling under both the heads of compensation are not exhaustive in nature but only illustrative.
It is also necessary to state here that no amount of money or compensation can put the injured/claimant exactly in the same position or place where he was before the accident and an effort is to be made only to reasonably compensate her or to put her almost in the same place or position where he could have been if the alleged accident had not taken place and this compensation is to be assessed in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The object of compensating her is also not to reward her or to make her rich in an unjust manner.
It is also well settled that the 'just' compensation to be awarded to the claimant has to be calculated objectively and it may involve some guess work in calculating the different amounts which the claimant may be entitled under the different heads of compensation.
Further, in case of permanent disability, the assessment of compensation under the head of loss of future earning, would depend upon the effect and impact of such permanent disability on his earning capacity.
Reference in this regard can be made on some of important judgments on the subject like the judgment in the case of R.D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India)
